title: How Brazil’s ‘labor revolution’ pushed an aspiring middle class to the political right
text:
How Brazil’s ‘labor revolution’ pushed an aspiring middle class to the political right
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva built his political movement on workers’ rights and social mobility. Ahead of the presidential runoff, that might not be enough anymore.
For nearly five decades, Betim, an industrial city with factories sprawled across rolling hills, embodied working-class aspirations in Brazil, which in turn undergirded the leftist political movement of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
But, when local Guilherme de Souza recently landed a job in machine maintenance at the Stellantis automotive factory on the edge of this industrial town, it was far from his dream job. Instead, he’s attending a night course, with plans to become an entrepreneur running his own car repair business – and most importantly, to work for himself.
His attitude reveals a shift in the demographic with whom the left built its success on promises of secure jobs and worker protections, especially in a place like Betim, which exploded due to factory work but now sees its community’s ambitions changing. Today, working-class Brazilians want not simply better jobs, but to be their own bosses.
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva built his political movement on speaking to Brazil’s poor and working classes. Ahead of the presidential runoff, workers say his party has lost touch with its aspirations.
That modern notion of success could reshape Brazil’s politics ahead of Sunday’s presidential runoff.
Lula, as the president is known here, cut his political teeth as a union leader in the 1970s, and built his leftist movement on the hopes of Brazil’s working class. But over the course of his three nonconsecutive presidential terms – he’s running for his fourth – the realities for poor and middle-class Brazilians have dramatically changed. His Workers’ Party (PT) now seems out of touch with workers whose goals have been shaped by previous Lula policies that lifted millions out of poverty, recent economic downturn, and the arrival of social media platforms, where coaches promote social mobility through hard work and meritocracy.
Lula earned 3.3 million fewer votes in this year’s first-round election than he did in the 2022 vote. Analysts say support has been primarily lost among the country’s “C class” – largely urban, aspiring middle classes earning between 2,525 and 10,885 reais per month, or about $503-$2,150.
“When you look at the numbers, you see that it is the independent micro-entrepreneur who is switching” from the political left to the right, says Rosana Pinheiro-Machado, professor of global studies at University College Dublin in Ireland. And the emergence of app-based gig work and digital entrepreneurship, accelerated by the pandemic, caused a “labor revolution” in Brazil, which Lula’s PT has struggled to keep up with, she says.
Looking for “renovation”
Right-wing Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro is projected to earn 48% of this weekend’s runoff vote, according to an Ideia/Meio poll published Oct. 21. Lula polled with 46% of support. But that gap widens among voters who see running their own business as a life improvement: 62.3% support Mr. Bolsonaro, and 33.5%, Lula.
Lula’s first two terms in office, between 2003 and 2010, are remembered for his welfare programs that pulled tens of millions of people out of poverty, giving them access to new consumer goods – and the opportunity to reach for new life goals.
But as the country faced an economic and political crisis in the mid-2010s, this ascendant middle class “often remained on the margins of the formal [labor] market, aspiring to more, but frustrated,” says Dr. Pinheiro-Machado. Brazil has a historically large informal sector, now numbering nearly 39 million people.
Talk of reprising “Lula 1,” and the deployment of widespread social spending when he clinched the presidency for a third term in 2023, has failed to resonate with this more modern working middle-class today.
That is evident in Betim, a low-rise city of nearly half a million people sliced in two by a busy highway. It owes its growth to the arrival of a Fiat plant in 1976, which later became Stellantis in a 2021 merger. Betim’s thriving industrial sector employs tens of thousands of salaried workers today. But the number of registered micro-entrepreneurs here has exploded in the past decade, with 7,750 new micro-entrepreneurs registering in 2025, bringing the total close to 37,000 self-employed locals.
The “small-business owners, they’re saturated; they want renovation,” says George Sergio Rosa, president of the local chapter of G10 Favelas, a national social impact organization here.
From its primrose-yellow headquarters in a low-income neighborhood that mushroomed across the highway from the Fiat plant as Betim’s industrial development attracted people looking for work, G10 Favelas runs programs to help youth enter the workforce. It holds recruitment drives for big firms like Stellantis and organizes courses for entrepreneurs to learn new skills, like digital marketing.
Young people no longer see the appeal of a salaried job with fixed hours, Mr. Rosa says. He hears regularly how the favela’s hundreds of small-business owners – from barbers to cooks – say they feel burdened by high taxes.
“The PT has always focused on the well-being of the worker,” he says. Just last week, a landmark labor reform was approved by Congress and championed by the Lula government, for example, shortening the workweek to 40 hours and increasing compulsory rest days, without cutting salaries.
But those policies don’t speak to small entrepreneurs, who see them as obstacles for their work, Mr. Rosa says. He sees this cohort as leaning more to the right.
Even on the factory floor, “thousands of workers who were benefited by federal government programs don’t feel represented by Lula,” says Alex Custodio, president of the metalworkers union for Betim and surrounding cities. It comes down, in part, to this desire so many Brazilians have today of working for themselves, he says. According to the latest Global Entrepreneurship Monitor report, 40% of Brazilians dream of having their own business, and 43 million plan on becoming entrepreneurs within the next three years – the world’s second-largest cohort, behind India.
“It’s been 18 years [of PT governments], and we just see more of the same,” says Mr. de Souza, the mechanic and aspiring entrepreneur. He plans to vote for Mr. Bolsonaro.
Dignity and visibility
The far right has successfully tapped into this discontent, attacking welfare policies and extolling individual responsibility, which resonates with many self-employed workers, says Dr. Pinheiro-Machado.
Gig workers in Betim, like Jackson Santos, a motorcycle driver, say they made the switch from formal employment in search of more autonomy and better pay.
“If someone wants to keep working in a supermarket their entire life, that’s their choice,” Mr. Santos says. “But the quality of life that I aspire to, God willing – I want to travel, see other countries, have a family. I can’t do that while earning 3,000 reais,” about $595.
Mr. Santos earns roughly twice that as a courier, while he makes extra as an influencer online, where he has amassed hundreds of thousands of followers by posting videos of himself doing courier work in a suit and tie, earning the nickname “motoboy elegante.”
A desire for respect and recognition underpins workers’ motivations for entrepreneurship. “The Brazilian working class was one of the world’s most humiliated and marginalized,” says Dr. Pinheiro-Machado, who has studied inequality in the Global South. Behind the pursuit of online influence, and material comfort and wealth, she says, is a need for dignity and visibility.
An online following is something Betim native Jhonatan Barbosa Alves aspires to, too. He’s trained as an electrotechnician, but recently went back to driving Ubers “until something better comes along.” He sells watches and perfume online and is trying to launch a gaming channel on social media.
Mr. Bolsonaro isn’t his first choice as a leader, but he’ll vote for him Sunday against Lula, he says. He identifies with Mr. Bolsonaro’s defense of conservative values, and likes his talk of reassessing benefits payments and support for entrepreneurs.
While the left struggles to signal what it can offer this new breed of worker today, says Dr. Pinheiro-Machado, “even if Lula wins, the far right has won the dispute for hearts and minds.”
